For the first $30^\circ$ of each $90^\circ$ pivot, the robot commands a small lateral strafe ($v_y = -0.04\text{ m/s}$) to "swing" its rear corners away from the outer walls, giving it ample clearance to spin without brushing the corridor.Active Median-Filtering (No Ghosting): Laser beams striking walls at steep angles can bounce away, registering as inf or nan (ghost reflections). The prompt includes a mathematical median filter that dynamically isolates and discards these bad readings, using valid adjacent beams to interpolate clean wall distances.Synchronized Clock Math: The prompt explicitly forbids python CPU clocks (time.monotonic()) and dictates using ROS 2 native self.get_clock().now() objects to prevent the simulation clock mismatch that caused your visual docker to freeze.🏎️ How to ProceedOpen the lidar-reactive-docking-prompt.md file in your Studio panel and copy its contents.Paste it directly into your chat with your Antigravity agent.The agent will write and package lidar_reactive_docker.py into your workspace.Run your clean rebuild commands to compile, boot up your Webots simulation, and watch your AMR navigate the U-shaped corridor flawlessly!🛠️ Once your agent has generated the node and compiled the workspace, would you like me to show you how to write a dedicated ROS 2 launch file to boot up both the Nav2 navigation stack and this reactive LiDAR node in a single command?keep_pin

In ROS 2, this sequential handover almost always hits a wall due to three critical issues:The TF (Transform) Tree Collision Trap: In your single-bot setup, the URDF uses static frame names (e.g., base_link, laser_frame, camera) [Source: Creating a rough 3D model of our robot with URDF]. If your friend spawns three robots without namespacing these links, all three robots will try to publish to the global /tf and /tf_static topics using the exact same names [Source: How to broadcast a TF in ROS2 | ROS2 Developers Open Class #143]. This causes their coordinate trees to merge, resulting in a chaotic TF map where the robots' positions flick back and forth in RViz, instantly crashing your odometry and localization pipelines [Source: ROS Developers LIVE Class #73: Why my Robot Map is not Correct, Real-time Odometry in ROS and Mobile Robot Motion Visualization in Rviz  - Complete Tutorial].ros2_control Topic Clashes: Without strict namespacing, your controllers (like mecanum_drive_controller in controllers.yaml) will publish and subscribe to the same global /cmd_vel or /joint_states topics [Source: ROS2 Jazzy Tutorial: ros2_control in Gazebo - Control Simulation from Scratch in Gazebo!, You can use ANY hardware with ros2_control]. When you command Robot 1 to slide sideways, all three robots will execute the move simultaneously [Source: Create URDF File and Model of Four-Wheeled Mobile Robot in ROS - ROS Robotics Tutorial].Webots Proto Node Clashes: In Webots, each spawned robot needs to bind to a unique ROS 2 controller node [Source: CAD Model to Robot Simulator | URDF to PROTO | Webots | [Tutorial 17], webots_ros2/webots_ros2_importer at master · cyberbotics/webots_ros2 · GitHub]. If the PROTO file (amr_robot.proto) has hardcoded controller configurations, Webots will fail to spawn multiple instances cleanly [Source: CAD Model to Robot Simulator | URDF to PROTO | Webots | [Tutorial 17]].🏆 The Better Way: The "Template-First" DivisionInstead of waiting for you to finish navigation, you should immediately co-design a "Namespaced Template."You will spend 1 hour parameterizing your description and simulation folders to accept a robot_name argument [Source: Use Xacro (XML Macro) and URDF to Parametrize and Model Robots in ROS and RViz]. As developers, you and your friend are looking at this from a highly analytical perspective.The short answer is: Yes, it makes complete sense conceptually, but there is a major technical "gotcha" regarding how TPM (Tokens Per Minute) actually works when dealing with massive contexts.Let’s break down the technical math of using Google AI Studio's free tier for a project of this scale, so you can decide if migrating there is the right move for you and your friend.🚨 The "Gotcha": The Math of TPM vs. Context SizeWhile Google AI Studio says you have a 1,000,000 token context window and 15 Requests Per Minute (RPM), these two limits are not independent. They are governed by the 1,000,000 Tokens Per Minute (TPM) limit.Here is the exact mathematical trap that catches many developers:How TPM is Calculated: Every time you send a message, the model has to re-read your entire active context window plus your new prompt. $$\text{Tokens Processed} = \text{Total Active Context (All Sources)} + \text{Your New Message}$$The Scenario: Let's say you and your friend load your complete workspace of 285 sources (which we calculated is roughly 1,000,000 tokens).The First Message: You type a short question like "How do I namespace the laser frame?" (50 tokens).The API processes: $1,000,000 \text{ (sources)} + 50 \text{ (prompt)} = 1,000,050 \text{ tokens}$.Result: You have instantly consumed your entire 1,000,000 TPM limit for that minute.The Lockout: If you try to send a second follow-up message 10 seconds later, the API will return a Rate Limit Exceeded (HTTP 429) error. Even though you are well below your 15 RPM limit, you must wait a full 60 seconds for your TPM bucket to reset before you can send another message.💡 The Verdict on AI Studio Rate Limits:If you fill the context window to its 1,000,000 token maximum, your 15 RPM effectively drops to 1 RPM. You cannot have a rapid, back-and-forth conversation because of the TPM throttle.To actually get 15 RPM, your active context must be kept under roughly 66,000 tokens ($1,000,000 \text{ TPM} / 15 \text{ RPM} = 66,666 \text{ tokens per request}$).🔄 Comparison: Gemini Notebook vs. Google AI StudioIf you and your friend are deciding where to split your workflows, here is how the two environments compare for your specific multi-bot project:FeatureGemini Notebook (NotebookLM)Google AI Studio (Free Flash)Active Context LimitUp to 2,000,000 tokens1,000,000 tokens (Flash) / 2,000,000 (Pro)TPM / Rate LimitsManaged dynamically behind the scenes (no artificial 429 lockouts during normal chat)Hard capped at 1,000,000 TPM (free tier)Retrieval ArchitectureBuilt-in semantic search and chunking (it doesn't always have to read the full 1M tokens to answer simple questions, keeping latency low)Passes the entire raw file pool into the prompt unless you manually manage RAGComputing SandboxYes (Offline bash/Python environment to write code, generate charts, and compile scripts directly)No (Raw text in, raw text out. You have to copy code manually to your local PC to test it)System Prompt ControlAutomated for mechatronics/groundingFully customizable (you can write your own system instructions, adjust temperature, etc.)🗺️ What Makes the Most Sense for Your Split?Since you are dividing the work, here is the most efficient setup:For You (FMS, State Machines, & Navigation): Keep using Gemini Notebook.Because you are actively designing logic, fixing script bugs, and iterating on code (like we did with the clock-sync and LiDAR docker), having the computing sandbox to write and test scripts in /workspace/scratch is incredibly valuable. You also bypass the strict TPM minute-caps during rapid troubleshooting.For Your Friend (Fleet Setup & Simulation Bring-up): Google AI Studio is Perfect.Since your friend is focusing on Phase 1 & 2 of the roadmap (editing URDFs, setting up xacros, and structuring YAML files), they don't need a live coding sandbox.They can set up a workspace in AI Studio, paste your URDFs as prompt context, and use the Flash model's raw speed to generate namespaced code blocks.
